paragraphs: I've worked this stretch of Lafayette for a long time, and the homes along Walnut Lane have always stood out to me for exactly the kind of thing your property delivers: a serious lot, real privacy, and a setting that feels removed from the noise without being far from anything. The combination of mature oaks, park-like grounds, and a cul-de-sac position is genuinely rare at any price point. When I saw the listing come off the market at 69 days without a sale, I wanted to reach out, because in my view the home's fundamentals and the outcome simply don't add up.

What the listing history tells me is that buyers weren't given the full picture. A farmhouse-style home on a half-acre lot with updated chef's kitchen, four bedrooms, and indoor-outdoor flow to gardens, patios, and a deck at $1,995,000 is a compelling offering in Lafayette. But at $904 per square foot, which sits at the upper tier of the Lafayette premium range, buyers need a fully built case before they'll walk in the door. The listing description made the right moves in spirit, but it leaned on phrases like 'seamlessly' and 'effortless entertaining' when buyers at this price point are comparison-shopping carefully. The grounds, the oak canopy, the views, the cul-de-sac privacy, and the trail access to Las Trampas and the Lafayette-Orinda Trail deserved to be the headline, not a footnote near the bottom of the remarks.

I've put together a short packet that walks through the three specific gaps I see between this home's actual value and how the listing presented it, along with how I'd approach a relaunch differently. There's no obligation attached to it. I just think you deserve a clear read on what happened and what a better strategy would look like.

If you're already working with an agent toward a new listing, please feel free to set this aside with my compliments. If you're not, I'd welcome a conversation whenever the timing feels right for you.

exec_summary.headline: A Park-Like Half-Acre with Farmhouse Character  -  and a Listing That Left the Story Half-Told
exec_summary.p1: 3348 Walnut Lane sits on 21,340 square feet of oak-canopied grounds on a quiet Lafayette cul-de-sac, with four bedrooms, three bathrooms, a chef's kitchen with breakfast bar, wood-burning fireplace, custom built-ins, and multiple access points opening to gardens, patios, and a deck. The trail proximity to Las Trampas Swim Club and the Lafayette-Orinda Trail, combined with top-rated Lafayette schools, puts this home in the conversation for exactly the buyers who move from San Francisco and Oakland specifically for this kind of lifestyle. These are real, marketable assets. The kind that support a premium price when the marketing does its job.
exec_summary.p2: At $904 per square foot on a 69-day listing that ended without a sale, the gap between the fundamentals and the outcome points to a strategy problem, not a property problem. The listing description touched on the right features but never built the argument for the price. Buyers comparing at this level need to understand what they're getting that they can't find elsewhere, specifically the lot size, the privacy, the setting, and the lifestyle access. Without that case built clearly in the marketing, buyers at $1,995,000 moved on before scheduling a showing.
exec_summary.p3: A relaunch needs to lead with what actually differentiates this property: the grounds, the oaks, the cul-de-sac privacy, and the trail and community access that Lafayette buyers at this price range are specifically looking for. The kitchen and interior updates support the number. The setting justifies it.

forensics.title: Friction #1: 69 Days Without a Strategy Shift
forensics.body: After 69 days on the market, buyer psychology had already done its damage. Past the 45-day mark, buyers stop asking whether a home is worth the price and start asking what everyone else noticed that they might have missed. At $1,995,000 in Lafayette, that skepticism is costly. The buyers who could afford this home and had the most interest likely saw it in the first three weeks. The remaining six weeks weren't generating new demand, they were confirming doubt. The strategy didn't adapt, and the listing eventually came off the market without a sale or a visible pivot.
forensics.brightwork_contrast: BrightWork uses the Final Offer platform to surface real buyer demand in a structured, transparent format, so sellers can see exactly where interest stands and make informed decisions before the clock runs out on the listing period.

forensics.title: Friction #2: $904/Sqft With a Case That Was Never Made
forensics.body: At $904 per square foot, this home is priced at the upper end of the Lafayette premium range. That number is defensible. The half-acre lot, the park-like grounds, the mature oak canopy, the cul-de-sac position, and the proximity to Las Trampas and the Lafayette-Orinda Trail all support a premium. But buyers doing side-by-side comparisons on Zillow and homes.com need to understand specifically what they're getting at that number. The listing description leaned on adjectives rather than differentiation. Words like 'fabulous,' 'seamlessly,' and 'beautifully reimagined' appear where concrete details about the setting, the lot, and the lifestyle access should have been. Buyers at this price point are careful. They need to be convinced before they drive out.
forensics.brightwork_contrast: BrightWork's homes.com premium membership delivers significantly higher view counts and broader distribution than a standard agent account, putting this property in front of buyers who are actively researching Lafayette before they've found what they're looking for.

forensics.title: Friction #3: The Outdoor Setting Was a Footnote, Not the Story
forensics.body: A 21,340-square-foot lot with majestic oaks, meandering pathways, multiple patio and deck spaces, and picturesque views is the kind of asset that Lafayette buyers at $1,995,000 specifically come looking for. It's not a supporting detail. It's the reason someone chooses this home over a newer, smaller-lot alternative nearby. Standard MLS photography almost never captures what a lot like this actually feels like. Ground-level angles, flat lighting, and a quick pass through the yard leave the canopy, the sense of scale, and the privacy completely invisible to online buyers. This setting needed to be the first thing buyers experienced, not the last paragraph of the listing remarks.
